utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Loukas, I take it we can ask the usher to bring the witness in so that you can --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you're ready so that we could ask the usher to bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's just a matter I need to place on the record before we commence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time would that take? Because it usually takes a minute for the usher to get the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, it would probably take about three minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, then we'll wait for a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Firstly, in relation to Your Honour's comments at the end of the last session in relation to the 60-per cent guideline and approximately two hours remaining for the cross-examination. The first point I'd like to make, Your Honour, is that in the circumstances where we are dealing with a report that refers to something in the nature of 500 documents, Your Honour, the -- the question of the 60-per cent guideline applying in those circumstances, I would submit, is inappropriate. And -- and also, subtracting the time taken for Trial Chamber's questions from the time in question, I would submit, in those circumstances is also inappropriate. Of course, when the Trial Chamber at the end asks questions, the -- both parties are asked if they wish -- if any questions arise or what have you. So nevertheless, if the Trial Chamber's questions arise during the evidence in chief of the witness, then in those circumstances, I would submit particularly in the context of the expert report, Your Honour, the application -- the strict application of the 60-per cent guideline is not, in my submission, in the interests of justice or, in my most respectful submission, of a -- a fair trial. In addition, Your Honours will note that on the first day this witness commenced giving evidence not only were the -- were there question of the documents associated with the report, there were also a list of additional documents that the Prosecution took the witness through, documents, of course, in the main that are already in the evidence but nevertheless not part of necessarily the preparation in relation to this witness, who was meant to be dealt with in accordance with his report. And Your Honour did make some comments about the additional documents and the late service in relation to the exhibits list on the Defence on that question. The other aspect is this, Your Honour: This question of spending time on the -- the 16th Session, as it were. Your Honour, Mr. Harmon spent a significant amount of time taking the witness through selected and selective quotes and building upon them in relation to the evidence of this witness. And, Your Honour, in the circumstances, it's appropriate, I would submit, that the Defence also be given the opportunity to go through the 16th Session, particularly in the nature of the fact that it is a public trial, so that not only do the public have the benefit of the selected quotes that were dealt with by the Prosecution but also an opportunity to see the other perspective. The other question is this, Your Honour: Your Honour made some comments yesterday afternoon about the question of the first 30 minutes or so of my cross-examination. I reviewed that portion of the transcript last night, and they were questions related to independence, bias, the limitations of the expert's report, and the limitations of his expertise. These are classically important areas to explore, Your Honour, with any report of this nature. Unless Your Honour would be saying, "Ms. Loukas, there's no need to proceed into those questions because we've already found that the witness is not entirely impartial" or "that we already know how limited his expertise is," only in those circumstances where Your Honours had already made that finding could Your Honours say that any exploration of issues of independence or limitations of expertise could in any way be inappropriate for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the main issue is that it all can be done in approximately a third of the time you take for it. When the Prosecution takes its time to draw our attention to certain portions, then, of course, if they spend time on that, that would create time for the Defence as well. Let's -- let's proceed. It's -- it was also about the -- there were a lot of -- of issues, perhaps even during the whole first hour of the cross-examination, where the whole of the Chamber thought if it has to be addressed - and it's of course entirely up to the Defence to do it or not to do it - then let's do it as efficiently as possible and not spend -- as I said yesterday, after ten minutes we were wondering what the issue was. Please come to your point as quickly as possible. And if you say for bias, could you please -- this and this and this. But we get an introduction of five or ten questions which is all an access to the issue. The Chamber would very much like the parties to come to the issue right away. And I do know that it's -- advocacy is an art, as I do understand, but sometimes a little bit less artistic would certainly save time. Let's not spend too much time on it. If there's really something which is so vital that you'd like to further elaborate on it, take the next minute, and then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the only point I would make is this: If you were to say that all this could be done more quickly and more efficiently, then I think that that's something that could in the most strenuous terms also be emphasised to the Prosecution, firstly. And I understood that your comments did apply to both, firstly. And secondly, my major concern is this, Your Honour: That the -- the question of scheduling and the completion strategy has placed such a burden, in my respectful submission, in terms of ensuring that there is an effective defence and fair trial for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand your point. I'm not going to say more about it. It never happened that the Chamber after ten minutes did not have any idea on what the Prosecution was seeking to establish. Let's -- I take it -- and, of course, the Chamber is aware that you feel that there's an extreme strain that we are working within certain time limits set by the Chamber; not by the completion strategy but by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will make this comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The evidence in chief of the witness extended over two and a half days. His evidence began on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- if they take much time, then 60 per cent is more -- is more time as well. But let's not -- let's just proceed and see that we can use our time now, at least, to hear whatever the witness can tell us. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I again would like to draw your attention to the binding character of the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. It is still valid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Loukas. How are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I have very limited time to deal with you this morning. So in terms of the questioning, if you -- if there is a question that you can answer "yes" or "no" to, or "I don't know" or what have you, the shorter the better.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, I was just taking you through the 16th Session, you'll recall, yesterday evening. And I, in fact, just want to take you to, firstly, a certain portion of the 16th Session, and we'll do this very quickly. And it's at page 41 in relation to the comments made by Mr. Mladic. And you will recall that you were referred to a certain portion of his speech, where he was dealing with -- "We cannot cleanse nor can we have a sieve to sift so that only Serbs would stay or that Serbs would fall through and the rest leave." He also further went on to say -- he talked about, in fact, going to his own village where he was born. And -- you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This -- is that the section after his -- his speech? Yes, I do -- I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. And -- and indeed he indicated that -- basically that "both Serbs and Muslims all must take care of one another."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's found on page 39 of the tabbed version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm much obliged to Mr. Harmon. That will make it a lot faster, seeing we're working from two versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, moving along in terms of the 16th Session, we go to the contribution of Mr. Krajisnik, which is at page 51 of my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That could well be at page 49, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that is, in fact, that Mr. Krajisnik indicated that -- he was basically summarising the discussion thus far, and he indicates "This was a proposal about choosing between the option of war and the political option. I think that we should choose the political option and the option of war always comes what is imposed upon us. But in reality if we are establishing an army, it means that we do expect the war option." Now, just in relation to the comments of Mr. Krajisnik there, it's quite clear that he's still in favour of settling things through the political process, but then -- but nevertheless the war is there and they have to be in a position to defend themselves; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't necessarily agree with that assertion. Mr. Krajisnik later on in that section discusses -- in fact, he says, "We are at war." It's not that they're not at war. And also, he makes reference to the fact that once they have their Serbian army, it will be able to -- it will be easier to achieve the -- presumably the goals that they have been discussing earlier on, now that they have their army and that they could have done that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Which particular portion are you referring to, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my one, I've got page 51 at the top "We are at war. It will be possible to solve these things with the Muslims and Croats only by war. Politics will be the -- and the politics will be instrumental in bringing it to an end and I don't know whether I've encompassed everything." And then he says a little bit later: "Please, if we acquire the territories which we agree on and have conceived of today plus the Corridor we get up there, we will have done this generation -- we'll have done so much for the Serbian people and this debt will be impossible to repay."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. You've been through that. But Mr. Brown, you understand that, of course, text such as this are possible -- it's possible to have alternative -- an alternative analysis other than the one you put forward. You understand that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You know, texts generally have --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, in fact, if you look at this statement, "We are at war" is a statement of the obvious. A war was proceeding, was it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conflict had broken out in Bosnia, yes, as -- as -- as I think I indicated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And he also makes the -- the statement that "It's important for Serbs to be rational."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you direct me to that section? I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A couple of lines lower.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's just a couple of lines below. "But it must be the rational Serbs who are leading the Serbian people today."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he says that there.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And there's actually nothing wrong with defending your own territory if you're under attack, is there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying that as a hypothetical question or are you talking about this particular case here?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm asking you as a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as a hypothetical question, I'm sure there's nothing wrong with defending your own territory if you're under attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving on, there's also a section there, you'll recall, that Mr. Krajisnik indicates that -- there must not be looting and what have you. I think it's just before that portion I took you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 50, Your Honours, Counsel. Toward the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And if we go on to page 54 in my version - that's page 52 in your version - Mr. Krajisnik is speaking again, and he indicates "This is the final proposal. I swear I shall abide by the constitution and the laws of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I shall protect its constitutional system honourably and faithfully, respecting moral standards and spiritual values in the struggle for the freedom of the entire Serbian people and all other citizens of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina so help me God." So in relation to that particular proposal being put forward there by Mr. Krajisnik, it's quite clear that the "Serb" in Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is to include people other than Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what he's reading out there, whether that's a -- some kind of standard constitutional text or loyalty, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think they're formulating the text of an oath to be taken by all organs, so ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would only say if that's what he said, as a -- as a formulation of an oath, then that's what he's saying. But I would maybe balance that with what seemed to happen in the months succeeding this Assembly and had already happened apparently in some municipalities in the months -- or the weeks prior to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, that's your analysis, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it seems to me that the documentation indicated that a large number of non-Serbs in the Serbian Republic were not there and that this was not a republic that did indeed seem to protect all other citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, do you find it impossible to canvass a view that doesn't accord with the view expressed in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, clearly I -- I don't find it impossible. I mean, as I said, there are certain limitations to the report I set. It was based very heavily on documentation, very heavily on documentation from the Krajina Corps and other military-related documentations. I've highlighted those limitations. So clearly if there's other documentation around that would seem to go against that, I would be more than happy to -- to review that material and, where necessary, make any adjustments, and I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm not just talking about other documentation, I'm talking about the documentation you've seen. Is it possible for you -- for example, in your report, you -- when you're examining a document, you will give it a particular slant, one that favours the Prosecution more than it does the Defence. Is it possible for you -- and, in fact, I'd be interested in your response to this, why in your report you didn't posit an alternative analysis on the various documents as an impartial expert rather than one that just accorded with the Prosecution theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to object to that, Your Honour. The witness -- we went over that yesterday about the Prosecution theory. The witness said he was not familiar with the Prosecution theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I will leave that alone, Your Honour. If -- if the witness, who's been working in the OTP office from 1998 to 2004, does not know the Prosecution theory, then I will leave that where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll object to that, Your Honour. That's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I withdraw that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, let's go to the combat readiness report, which is tab 6. Now, in relation to the combat readiness report, when you analyse a document like that, which is an ex post facto report of the previous year, do you, in analysing that, take into account the fact that this is, of course, a secondary source, as opposed to a primary source of the information contained therein?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's actually a primary-source document, obviously, because it's come from -- from the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could we agree on the following: It is a primary report to the extent that it comes direct from the source that drafted it and at the same time it includes a lot of information which may have been -- may have been collected by other primary sources? It's -- I mean, it seems totally clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, that's where I'm leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's actually a combination of both, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a primary-source document that's making comments on activities that have happened prior to the writing of the document. Many documents do that. You could say that some of the police documents that were reporting on the camps are in the same position; they're summarising what had happened in a municipality a week or two or a month before. So it's a primary-source document, but its content is about -- well, its context actually is somewhat multifaceted. It's both looking back at what happened in 1992; it's highlighting some weaknesses; and it's making recommendations about what they're going to do in the -- in the future. So it's actually a somewhat multifaceted document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's approach the document from another angle. It is, of course, a document that any military analyst would also have to analyse conditions on the ground and have evidence in relation to conditions on the ground to compare with what is in the report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, of course, you were not there, so you can't be in a position to comment on the accuracy or otherwise of what is in the report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree there because there are references in the report that clearly relate to documentation and activities that occurred at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But you can't vouch for each and every aspect of the report on combat readiness, can you, as a military analyst.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, it goes without saying that if the witness was not there, if it says there were 500 mortars here or 300 mortars there, what this expert can do is to see whether he finds any support for such positions taken in this document in other documents, but it's clear that he wasn't there, that he hasn't seen with his own eyes the 500 mortars or the 200 rifles or the one hand-grenade. That's really -- it goes, for the Bench, without saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, okay, as a military analyst, in terms of analysing a report of this nature, it's clear, is it not, that you would have to be very careful to look at and ensure that there were other corroborative sources in relation to a specific piece of information, as opposed to perhaps some rhetoric or ex post facto boasting or attempting to make the situation look better than it had been?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you would have to be wary that that was not going to come into the document, but I would have to say that in looking at this document -- well, first of all, the document is not a completely rosy document. It does highlight some significant problems that they faced and continued to face in the document. So that's one.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, you haven't finished your answer. Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there are a significant number of references in this document that you can tie back to documentation from 1992 and when they comment about issues, that you can link back to -- to successes, directives. They talk, for example, about the two-stage development of the army. And that would seem to have been borne out by the documentations more contemporaneously in 1992. So having looked at the document, it seems that, you know, it is -- it is not a, you know, a rose-tinted view of the VRS. They do highlight some difficulties they have, difficulties they had in 1992 as well as difficulties they still have in 1993. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I think there are a lot of references in there that you can tie back to, issues from 1992 or documents from 1992, which for me seem to corroborate the document. Also, the document itself is a -- you know, highly confidential document, a strictly secret document, which seems to have some significance as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Actually, going to that document, specifically going to communications and what you've said there about -- what's been said there about communications, clearly, to rely on the document, you would have to have -- you would have to look at other evidence on the ground as to what the state of communications was, would you not, during the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would presumably have to look back in 1992 to see if -- if some of the issues that they discussed there were -- were put in place. And having looked at the military documentation, it appears that they did have a good communication system. They themselves in the 1992 -- sorry, the 1993 document said the -- they admit they had problems. They admit they had difficulties at the beginning of the war. They admit that the military had to be relied on quite heavily for the use of communications, but they appear to have overcome those communication problems. They outline how they did that. They outline the uses that they made of the existing systems that were there, and they come to the conclusion that the communication system was very good. And when I look back at 1992 and see that the 1st Krajina Corps was able to transmit messages, was able to pass message documents down the chain, was made aware of meetings they had to attend to, was able to conduct large-scale military operations in a very short space of time, the Operation Corridor being a good example: A two-corps operation involving units of the MUP from Knin, a large, large amount of forces, it was able to mount that operation in an unbelievably short space of time and it was able to be successful in that operation in a space of a week to ten days, and I would argue that that indicates to me that they did, in fact, have very good communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, of course, developing a communications -- system for communication within the army sphere itself is critical, is it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to move on to your errata sheet, which I think is tab 2 in folder 1. In fact, tab 3. Do you have that, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to your -- the first page of your errata sheet, you have a number of errata there in relation to paragraphs 1.113 of your report and paragraph 1.114 of your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, those matters that you've included in your errata sheet were, of course, matters that arose when you were being cross-examined in the Brdjanin trial; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Some of them.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, the very first one for paragraph 1.113, that arose during your cross-examination in the trial against Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the very next one, 1.113 arose in that context?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The misspelling of "Radoslav" does not concern us. On to paragraph 1.114, that also arose in your cross-examination in the trial against Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, when we look at what's actually contained there, in that passage of your report in relation to 113, you'd actually indicated there that -- towards the bottom of the paragraph on page 49 of your report -- "Decisions --" "Decisions relating to the establishment of civilian authorities and issues in relation to camps." That's the particular portion of the report that we're dealing with. Now, you were actually taken to that during your cross-examination, and it was quite clear, was it not, in reference to your footnote that it was not issues in relation to camps but, rather, a discussion relating to the work of the Red Cross. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'd like to possibly see the document. I -- I cannot remember the discussion in the Brdjanin case itself. I can tell you what the footnote was from the -- from my report, and I'm assuming the ICRC were visiting the camps and it was relating to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Brown, are you saying that -- firstly, when did you prepare this errata sheet?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared those two -- or I think it was two or three sections. I actually had noted in a copy of my report not long after the Brdjanin case when I looked at it and reviewed it that I had -- there was a small -- there were some small errors which may have been misinterpreted. And in order to include those in the report, I wrote those on the side of -- of my report, not long after the Brdjanin testimony. So I'm not sure when that was. 2003, I think. The errata sheet here was prepared by me about two weeks ago, ten -- not as much as that. Maybe about ten days ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when I looked at the errata sheet, there had been one or two ERN numbers, for example, I noted an ERN was wrong, I included that in and I --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm not cross-examining you about the ERN numbers. I'm cross-examining you about paragraph 1.113 and the assertion that you had in your report that "Decisions relating to establishment of civilian authorities and issues in relation to camps" is in your text. You were cross-examined about it in the Brdjanin trial and it was quite clear that what was in your text was an overstatement in relation to your footnote, was it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was overstatement. Maybe it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Potentially misleading, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it was misleading at all. What I wanted to do in the errata was to tidy it up and make it slightly more clear. So maybe it was less clear and Mr. Brdjanin had made a point, which I think he had the right to do so, did, and when I reviewed the document, I decided to make a change to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you don't concede that it was potentially misleading to state in your report that there were "decisions relating to the establishment of civilian authorities and issues in relation to camps" when it was a discussion about the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to see the document in its context, whether it is a document saying the ICRC have visited camps and -- I know the ICRC did visit camps from other documentation. I know the ICRC visited Manjaca camp. And where it said "issues relating to camps," I wanted to tidy that up. I don't think it was misleading, and the whole context of the paragraph was to highlight that there were discussions with civilian authorities on a range of topics. And -- but when I -- when I reviewed that particular phrase "and issues in relation to camps," I agreed that it may not have been quite accurate, and hence my reason to put in an errata. I don't think it diminishes from the overall thrust of the paragraph, which was that at the regional level there was military and civilian cooperation and they discussed an array of topics. But as I say, my report is a -- a long one; it has many footnotes. In this case, Mr. Brdjanin raised that issue. When I reviewed it again, I realised that I might not have been as neat with my wording, and when I reviewed it after the testimony, I made some notes to that effect and then put that in the errata sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Moving on to the next topic. Paragraph 113, another matter that you included on your errata sheet as a result of your cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman in Brdjanin, you'd left the potentially misleading impression in your report in the text that -- and the phrase, I think, was -- what you've corrected there is "It was members of the ARK Crisis Staff accompanied the visit," and it should have read "representatives of the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina accompanied the visit." Again, that was potentially misleading that you were including the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was potentially erroneous to put it like that and I made the errata, as again one of the -- when I looked at the notes, I reviewed that, read the document again, and hence my putting in the errata sheet that -- however I've expressed it in the errata sheet, "members of the -- representatives of the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina accompanied the visit," rather than as it's written there.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Had you not been cross-examined on the comparison between your text and your footnotes, this would never have made it into the errata sheet, would it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you whether it would have made it in or not. If I had highlighted it and reread the document and reread the footnotes and realised there was a difficulty there, I would have put it into an errata sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we conclude it as a fair chance that it would not have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fair chance, Your Honour. I am being very honest, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, we expect honesty. Mr. Brown, prior to coming here to give evidence in the trial against Mr. Krajisnik, did you check your text as against your footnotes to ensure that you have been as accurate as possible in attempting to assist the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not checked the text against every footnote prior to coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to paragraph 114. There you say -- this was, again, something you were cross-examined about in the Brdjanin trial -- that "ARK Crisis Staff members toured the areas of combat activity and were briefed by military personnel." And as a result of being cross-examined on this by Mr. Ackerman, it was quite clear that it was not members, plural, of the ARK Crisis Staff; it was just Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin touring the area of combat activity.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite true because Stojan Zupljanin was also on a video in Kotor Varos, I believe, with Mr. -- with Mr. Brdjanin, and that -- so -- and there had also been visits. Mr. Radic, I know, who was on the Crisis Staff, had done a visit to Prijedor and, I think, Omarska camp. So there were indications that ARK Crisis Staff members did visit and tour the zone of responsibility. But what I wanted to do in this one in the errata sheet, was to tidy that up and put that it was Mr. Brdjanin in this particular case. But--

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's important, isn't it, to ensure that what's in your text and what you refer to in a footnote actually coincide and there is accuracy there. Is that not important?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But it is also important if you highlight -- highlight that there are errors, that you can rectify those, which I've done. And also, it doesn't get away from the main point that I was making. The ARK Crisis Staff members did tour the zone of responsibility, and there is video footage to that effect, documentary evidence to that effect, and that was the thrust of the paragraph and also the preceding paragraph about cooperation between military and regional figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Nevertheless, to be accurate, you had to correct it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I honestly corrected the -- the errors when I reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It added to the accuracy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, moving on. Let's go to a particular portion of your report. Let's go to the paragraph -- where is it? Page 22. And we're looking at footnote 41. We're looking at the paragraph, in fact, on page 21, paragraph 1.31. You've got a quote there, and you put it down to footnote 41.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I've got some copies here of footnote 41, which I'll distribute and so you can look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I take it that you want to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D48, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you have that document before you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber where in that report, the regular combat report that you have before you, that first part of the quote comes from.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to be in this document. I must have misreferenced the document. I do know a document from a daily combat report making reference to that does exist. I can attempt to get that and rectify the ERN and the footnote reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So that's an error.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Were you asked by the Prosecution to check your report after you'd finished giving evidence in the Brdjanin trial and before it was put forward in relation to this trial?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember being specifically asked that very direct question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Did you, as a responsible analyst wishing to ensure that the information you were conveying to the Trial Chamber was as accurate as possible, decide off your own bat to undertake that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of your question. Decide to -- to do what? Check the footnotes?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yeah. Make sure that your text is accurate and that your footnotes support what you have in the text.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this is a long report with a large number of footnotes. I admit that I had -- in this error, there is a referencing error. I am more than prepared to get the -- through the assistance of the Office of the Prosecutor, to get the accurate reference, because I know this document does exist with this quote and -- in order to rectify that error. This is a footnote -- a document with some 900 footnotes and clearly there are some small errors in there, and I don't think it detracts necessarily from what has been written and the thrust of my argument here in -- in that particular part of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to footnote 79, shall we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the Chamber would very much appreciate if the expert would retrieve from what document this quote comes. Would you please do that. And I take it, Mr. Harmon, that the material will be made available to the expert once he has finished his examination in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm undertaking right now, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- the retrieval of that right now because it may be that probably we can locate that document while Mr. Brown is still on the stand, and he can be examined about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you know, Mr. Harmon, that the Defence very much appreciates if experts find their own sources. But I think that if it's a literal quote, you would not object against Mr. Harmon being --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course not, Your Honour. No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the question is not that the quote may not exist in -- in some document but the question of the accuracy and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- research work of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But the Chamber then wants to know exactly from what document it is; time, source, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go to footnote 79, shall we? That's on page 29 of your report. And I have a copy of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that document would be what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D49, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Footnote 79. The quote that you've included on page 29 is -- ends with "They do not want anything that is somebody else's, anything that has not been theirs for centuries, but they will not give an inch of their own territory." Do you see that portion of the document that you've quoted there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In the actual document, there's a little bit further on, to place it in context, that it indicates there that "The peace-loving Serbian people care above all for peace and a peaceful and just settlement of all disputes in these areas. That is why their political leadership, organs, and institutions are persistently initiating negotiations on peaceful demarcation." Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I be provided with a copy of the document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it that it's just by mistake that you didn't receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I unfortunately ended up with -- I asked for six copies of every document and on this one I ended up with three for some reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I take it that the Chamber's copy would be available at this moment. We have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could you guide us to the page where --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It's on page 2 of the document itself. That's in relation to footnote 79.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "They will not give an inch of their own territory." You've gone up to there in your report, and you've excluded the quote I just read out to you, which includes "That is why their political leadership, organs, and institutions are persistently initiating negotiations on peaceful demarcation." Now, you left that out of the quote, Mr. Brown. Is that because it doesn't fit in with your overall thesis?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I didn't leave it out because it didn't fit with my overall thesis. I used the section relating to the constituent parts, the subject of the -- the paragraph is about the strategic goals being disseminated down into the military. And I think the negotiation issue is a separate issue to that. The section I've quoted indicates to me that the 1st Krajina Corps are making their soldiers aware that complete separation from the Muslim and Croat peoples is -- is their objective and their -- their goal, and that's -- that's what -- that's what I used the quote for.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But it's also important to include the fact that within this document the political leadership is persisting with initiating discussions -- or persistently initiating negotiations on peaceful demarcation. That's significant, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say -- and this wasn't what I was writing this particular part of the paragraph about.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that was not what I was writing that section and paragraph about.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, then for the complete picture, would then the lines that follow there, where the -- it's explained that "these peaceful efforts are not effective, blaming others for not accepting them, not appreciating them, the enemies of the Serbian people and of all the citizens are resolved to dictate conditions" -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if we need the whole of the context, then I would say that not only the -- the peaceful efforts but also the reasons why they are not successful in -- would then become relevant. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed. The statement where it says "The enemies of the Serbian people and of all of the citizens of the Serbian Republic --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "-- resolve to dictate conditions to the Serbian people with aggression, force, and weapons." I'm wondering if that's a mistranslation there. That doesn't ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, might be. I haven't got the original here. You know that I like to compare the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed you do, Your Honour. And indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you provide it to us, we could check it. If not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the original has been provided. It's in tab 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I can return Your Honour's document to you. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there was no need to ask for it, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Harmon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go to footnote 151.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I keep these documents or ...? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I'm in a position that we only have four copies of footnote 151, where we should have six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, as you know, we'll manage. Just distribute. We have four tables. Let's make sure that on every table there is a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Footnote 151, that's, in fact, in the text on page 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D50, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we go to footnote 151. That's on page 45. You indicate there that "In April 1992, Branko Djeric, president of the SRBiH government published instructions for the operations of crisis headquarters of Serb people in the municipalities, outlining some of the responsibilities of the Crisis Staffs, which included ..." Now, when you go down there to the one that you've included as the third one, "The command of the TO and the police force is under the exclusive authority of the professional staff," that basically means, does it not, "civilians stay out"?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem to indicate that, at paragraph 4, that there are professional staffs, that there's a military and TO staff, and to prevent interference, that the TO -- that that should happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And often that did seem to happen from the documentation that I've seen in -- in reviewing; although, there are examples where the Crisis Staff also did give some direct orders, I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But the instruction from on high there was that the civilians should basically butt out of what the TO and the police forces were doing, that it was a different area, that there was a division of function.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not quite sure I'd use the phrase "butt out." That seems to -- would imply that there's a certain unwelcome -- unwelcome relationship there. But it would seem --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: What they actually say there is "The command of the TO and the police forces is under the exclusive authority of the professional staff and therefore any interference regarding the command of the TO and/or the use of the police forces must be prevented." So they're saying "Stay away."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They seem to be indicating this division of responsibility, that there is presumably a police and a military and a -- and a political function --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in relation to commanding TO and police.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, of course, as -- as a military analyst writing a report, it may, in fact, have been useful to elucidate for the Trial Chamber that that's what that section there about professional staff meant.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I referenced that in the -- in the quote. It's -- it's there in the quote. I don't shy from that quote. And I think in -- if I can just read the next couple of pages very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "Professional staff" doesn't mean the same to everybody, does it? It's quite clear that this has a specific meaning that needs to be elucidated, doesn't it? Which you've just done.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't -- I don't think -- I think it speaks for itself, and I think in -- I think in -- in the -- the text of the report, which I produced that I say it wasn't envisaged that the Crisis Staffs were directly to command or order military units into combat action. But there are examples where that did seem to happen, Sanski Most being one that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just going to what you've left out of your quote, you actually left out that "The non-fighting population and the wounded must be treated in the most humane fashion and in accordance with the ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross. Prisoners of war also must be treated humanely and in accordance with the laws of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." You've left that out of your quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's which part exactly, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's paragraph 10, Your Honour, on page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's not in this section, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you've also left out paragraph 13: "War profiteers, gangs of looters, and similar shall be arrested and delivered to the investigating judicial organs of the Serbian Republic."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you've also left out 12: "It's imperative not to disturb commercial and other economic activities as long as their documentation is in order," et cetera, et cetera. You can read it for yourself there. That's an indication of the fact that a very important part of the Crisis Staff's function was to ensure that there was -- for example, there it refers to food rationing and what have you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- is there a question or are you just highlighting that issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm just highlighting what you've left out. You agree with me you've also left that out?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. As I say in this report, I'm not an expert in Crisis Staffs and there are others who know far more than I do in that area. The issue was to outline some of the responsibilities in relation to command, not relation to every single issue of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned issues of Geneva Convention, war profiteers, and looting in other parts of the report, but I'm not sure if it's -- the -- I haven't, as you say, included every single section of this document in that quote in paragraph 1.05.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And it's not because you're only including what suits your purposes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. The section is about outlining some of the responsibilities of the Crisis Staffs which relate to defence issues, and in particular command and control of the military and the relationship between the military. That seemed to be the salient points from this report. I've highlighted in the report that what it says is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, the -- the treatment of prisoners of war, that's -- and an instruction from on high in relation to in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, that's important, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's important. I'm sure all the sections are important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Brown, I think Ms. Loukas -- you said that you looked at the document from a military point of view and not on all aspects of the tasks of the Crisis Staff. Ms. Loukas asks you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. specifically now where you quoted the not interference with the commander of the TO, which apparently is a military matter, whether treatment of wounded and noncombatants and prisoners of war, whether that would not be also a specific military matter, that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it could do. But I think the section I was dealing with here was mainly about the relationship between the Crisis Staffs and the military. It wasn't necessarily about all the functions and roles of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But this is a military matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if you're talking about the relationship between Crisis Staff and the military, then this would be a subject that could be relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be relevant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, I just want to go on to footnote 180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, I take it that Mr. Harmon, since I didn't hear anything, does not object against using a different document on the footnote than ERN numbers, that is to say. You used a different translation. Let's just assume for practical purposes that it is the -- as if it was the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, about accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, what I've done with the DVD is I've just printed out the footnotes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In relation -- I've asked for the footnotes to be printed out. Not enough copies, obviously, but nevertheless ... But it seems that in that errata sheet there were a number of changes of ERNs noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, moving on to footnote 180. That's "Decisions and discussions on mobilisation." And I'll just distribute some copies of footnote 180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be number D51, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D51, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that particular document, it refers there to, at point 3, "Especially strict measures will be implemented against any person misusing the uniform and insignia of the police, the TO, Territorial Defence, or the army and without authorisation stopping or checking people's identity or vehicles, searching flats or other premises." So this was obviously, Mr. Brown, quite a problem, that people were running around wearing uniforms that were not entitled to and doing the sort of activities that are indicated there.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure in relation to this document whether you can draw that it was quite a problem. In relation to uniforms, I know at the 16th Assembly Session there was some emphasis placed on that "We all must have the same VRS insignia," I think was used, in order to -- you know, establishment of the army. So whether the issue of uniform is relating to the decision to establish the army a few days prior to this meeting or whether it's to do with, as you say, people wearing whatever they wanted, I can't tell, but clearly they want to ensure that everyone wears presumably the uniform of the VRS and wears the insignia of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's what you read from the document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think they're saying that strict measures should be taken to people misusing uniforms. So there either was a problem or they foresaw a problem, or they wanted to ensure that the decision of the 12th of May which established the VRS, and they talked about a common -- a common insignia and a common uniform, was employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're reading into that statement there that the complaint is -- let me see your answer again. "Clearly they wanted to ensure that everyone wears presumably the uniform of the VRS and wears the insignia of the VRS," and then you bring that back to the 12th of May, establishing the VRS. Mr. Brown, there's an alternative rational reading, is there not, of the document in question? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's three ways you could look at it in relation to uniforms. The first one is that people had been misusing uniforms and that they wanted to stop it. The second one, that they foresaw that there might be a problem and they wanted to make sure that they were putting down some marker to say that it wasn't going to be tolerated. Or thirdly, they're wanting to echo or re-echo what had been stated on the establishment of the VRS that everyone should wear the insignia of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. But your answer is that "I can't tell but clearly they want to ensure that everyone wears presumably the uniform of the VRS and wears the insignia of the VRS." That's your interpretation of that document; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think so. I think they want to make sure that people are not misusing the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on to another footnote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my proper understanding, Ms. Loukas, and you, Mr. Brown, I do understand that in 1.113 you describe how the military was seeking contact with civilian authorities, and also the other way round, that the civilian authorities were -- were involved in one way or the other, and the same was true for regional-level bodies, impacted on or were related to military activity. Did you specifically have paragraph 3 in mind here, or -- because I see a few other matters. "Urgent meetings should be called at all municipal secretaries of the Secretariat of National Defence. Talks should be held with General Talic about calling up and assigning military conscripts," which seems to be, at least, related to military activities. So I'm -- I'm just trying to understand what role this source plays in your report in the context of paragraph 1.113. We are now focussing especially on the interpretation of number 3 on this list; whereas, I - but please correct me if I'm wrong - reading this document, reading your report, it seems that you say this document shows that the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff had -- took decisions and had discussions that impacted on and were related to military activity. That's what your report says. And I do understand that you use this in support of that statement. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. This is one of a number of footnotes which I, I think, make that general point, that the 1st Krajina Corps was not completely divorced from the regional government, and when the regional authorities discussed and met and had conclusions, that some of those related and impacted on military issues. And this one is an example -- for example, point 5: "Talks should be held with General Talic about calling up and assigning a military conscript on 21st of May --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that gives a broader context to the interpretation of this document, then. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, 181 -- now, footnote 181.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'll just distribute footnote 181.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, we're on the same page, footnote 181. The point I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be D52?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D52, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you deal there with deadlines concerning the surrender of weapons. It's quite clear, isn't it, that we're dealing about the question of "The deadline that expired today has been extended at the request of the citizens of all nationalities because of the wish to return the weapons in a peaceful way and without the intervention of police." Now, just looking at that, of course, the -- it appears that the deadline applied to citizens of all nationalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On this document, it would seem to say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in some context, in reviewing the documentation, I didn't see any examples in the Krajina whereby the deadline to hand over legally held weapons was given to areas other than non-Serb areas. Deadlines were given in -- this deadline was extended, I believe, until -- or it was extended, at least. I think maybe even until the 18th. But it was extended and there are documentary references in Prijedor, in Sanski Most, in Novi, in Kljuc, in documents, and Crisis Staff documents and a knowledge of the military about those deadlines. And when those deadlines expired, invariably these areas were subject to military action. And I didn't see any examples whereby weapons were being handed in or military action was -- was being conducted in Serb areas, in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. But nevertheless, for the sake of accuracy, in relation to this question deadlines concerning the surrender of weapons, you've only quoted that particular document, and that's a document that applies to all nationalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the -- on -- on the reading of the document, it says that, but I would not say that that was what -- what seemed to happen after the expiration of these deadlines.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Let's move on to another footnote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, may I just ask, and may I also ask you,

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWN
utterances.text: Where does it say that it applies to all nationalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It actually says -- this is somewhat ambiguous: The deadline which was about to lapse was extended at the request of all citizens from ethnic groups. So in reality it's not -- it appears that the deadline is directed to all nationalities. It appears that the request to extend the deadline, if anything, has come from all national --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So a deadline has been set, of which we do not know to whom it was addressed, and now we see -- it may well be to all citizens or -- but, Ms. Loukas, I can't read this document that the deadline was set for all citizens. It doesn't say so, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in any event, it -- I think it can -- it's quite clear that the document is a document capable of more than one interpretation, is it not? And I think that's quite clear from the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It -- yes, it needs more. But in -- let me just -- I also see, by the way, on my screen that we are invited again to slow down. Ms. Loukas, you are talking later on about accuracy. But you said, "Now, just looking at that, of course it appears that the deadline applies to citizens of all nationalities; correct?" It doesn't appear at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I do say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do -- I do agree with you that the document would need some additional information. We'd need to know more about the deadline that was set. But it doesn't appear such. It appears that it was all ethnic groups that expressed the wish, but it doesn't say anything about to whom the deadline was addressed, from what I read at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just in relation to that, it's -- it's how I first read it, I must say, and interestingly enough, it's how the witness read it too. He said, "Yes, on this document it would seem to say so."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore it's good that the Chamber also reads.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe as a means of clarification, you know, re-reading the document, I agree, it doesn't state here who the weapon deadline or the handing of weapons deadline is targeted to. I believe that the initial deadline -- because this is saying that it's getting extended to the 14th. I believe the initial deadline was for the 11th, and that was as a result of an ARK -- or an -- actually a -- not an ARK but a regional National Defence instruction that went out on the 4th of May, which stated that: "All paramilitary formations and individuals in possession of illegal weapons and ammunition are tasked -- are asked to surrender these weapons and ammunition immediately, no later than 1500 hours on the 11th of May." But I do re-emphasise that in looking at the documentation and the expiration of this deadline, that the only areas that they were conducting military operations, often with the -- the description of seizing illegally-held weapons, were in non-Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Ms. Loukas, certainly the text, reading "the surrender of illegally-procured weapons," might need some further attention as well. What was considered to be -- what were considered to be illegally-procured weapons? Because we know how the different parties obtained weapons, how civilians obtained weapons. At least, we have heard quite some evidence on that. And I do understand that you consider that the deadline was also -- that at least -- well, let's assume if Serb civilians would have to hand in their weapons, that they would have been considered as illegally procured. Well, that raises a lot of questions. I just want to inform you that it's not as clear cut as it looks from your questions and even looks from the answers of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the -- the answer of the witness, Your Honour, was that the initial document indicated "all paramilitaries." I think that was the indication that he gave. But this is not an area that I want to spend a lot of time on, Your Honour. I'm actually looking at the question of the footnotes in quite some detail, because it's important in terms of the accuracy of the report, and I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas. We will adjourn until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, we're just going to go to page 61 of your report and to footnote 239. Now, I've distributed copies of that document. Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And had it been assigned a number already? I --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think it's about to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D53, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Has Mr. Brown got a copy of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you'll note that in the text of your report you indicate: "Some units were specifically ordered to take control of the territory and key facilities and to establish close links with the authorities." And the document you cite in that regard is footnote 239, and you have a copy of that document before you. If you could just point out for the Trial Chamber where it indicates "establish close links with the authorities."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure it does in this document, but there are many other documents I've reviewed. I think I'm using this footnote to reference securing key facilities, or the section on key facilities. I use other documents in the report which I discuss more widely in relation to close links with the authorities. In particular, the 21st of May Talic instruction after mobilisation, and there are a number of other documents in relation to ensuring close links with the authorities. But in this footnote, I am referring to securing facilities, and in particular I think I reference in paragraph 2 "The 30th Division, 6th Infantry Brigade and parts of the 343rd Motorised Brigade are redeployed in the area of direct use and are securing vital facilities within their units. "

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Brown, there's no doubt that this question of securing vital facilities is there, but in your text you indicate "close links with the authorities." We go to footnote 239, and in the document that you have cited that is actually not in the document, is it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I deal in this report with a fairly substantial section in relation to cooperation with the military and the -- and the -- the civilian authorities. It's referenced in a number of areas, and there are a lot of footnotes, I think, in the report. If I was to single out every single phrase and every single comment in this report and footnote it, I think the Judges would be spending a lot of time reading the report. It would be exceptionally unwieldy, exceptionally large. So it doesn't make reference directly to the issue of establishing close links. It does make reference to the issue of securing facilities, which is what I've used the footnotes for, and there are other areas in the report that deal with the issue of establishing close links.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, usually if one of your sources only relates to a portion of a sentence and not of the whole of the sentence, you do not hesitate to put the footnote somewhere half in the -- that sentence. Would you agree with me that if it's -- footnote 239 is not meant to support the establishment of close link with the authorities, then perhaps it should have been at a different place in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it could have been, Your Honour. Maybe it should have been moved to that section about securing units. I -- I think the report should be read in entirety and not necessarily with every single small issue footnoted or referenced. I could have possibly moved that to -- that footnote 239 to the area after "take control of territories," and put it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- maybe if I can assist the Court. I looked at my report during the break and -- in relation to footnote 41, which was an issue that Ms. Loukas raised earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not having access to the documents, it is possible that footnote 41 is the same as footnote 71.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I can stop you right there, Mr. Brown. During the break, Mr. Harmon gave me a document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Let's go back to this issue of 239 for a second, shall we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, then, that the Chamber sooner or later also gets it, because we asked specifically for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the document. I can distribute it, if Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I can also inform Your Honours that the document that is referenced and where the footnote was omitted by Mr. Brown, this document is also referenced in three other footnotes in his report; footnotes 109, 111, and 700.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, you understand, of course, how important it is that what you state in your text is accurate. You do realise that that's important, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether the witness says yes or no, Ms. Loukas, the Chamber is aware that it is important that accuracy is at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you yourself do realise the importance of ensuring that your footnotes connect with the text precisely.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the footnotes are there to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not further discuss the function of the footnote. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you use footnotes, they should be in the right place, they should support what is in the text, they should be as accurate as possible, and that's something that the Chamber knows already since they studied law themselves and had to use footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I won't deal with it any further, Your Honour, and I will leave the footnotes alone for the time being and move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to go to your phraseology in the report, in the text. Let's go to page 13 of your report, shall we? And let's go to paragraph 1.6, for example. You indicate there: "The threat posed by the Croats, however, was not only a perceived one but in some instances became very real." You could also have said, could you not, "The threat posed by the Croats was not only a perceived one but a real one," could you not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
