utterances.text: I -- I could have, but -- but I'm saying that in some instances it was very real, and in particular I'm highlighting Western Slavonia and I also, I believe, talk here about Bosanski Brod and Derventa. I'm sure there were other areas where the Croats were living where the threat may not necessarily have been real. So I'm highlighting a couple of instances where it was real. And I don't doubt that. I don't doubt that in Western Slavonia Croatian -- Croatian forces were -- were operating, and I don't doubt in Posavina that the area had been -- or the control of the territory had been taken over by Croat forces and that was a real threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Mr. Brown, that the phraseology you use somewhat diminishes the impact there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. Let's go to paragraph 1.12, where you indicate, about four lines down: "The JNA were in a position of exclusively assisting the Bosnian Serbs and the SDS and any attempt at balance, if it had genuinely existed, had gone." Now, why do you speculate there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My point is here that I argue that by April there had been this convergence, as indicated by the documentation. And when I say "genuinely --" "if it genuinely existed," I'm not sure that in the documents from late 1991 there would have been references to protecting the Serbs from genocide, but what I do say is that certainly by April this -- this convergence had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. But this phrase "attempt at balance, if it had genuinely existed..." I mean, you're not in a position to say that it had not genuinely existed, are you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I am in a position to say it may not have existed because the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That it never existed.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it genuinely existed -- I'm talking about some of the documentation in late 1991 and the Croatian war relating to that, which indicated that the objective of the JNA there was to protect the Serbs against genocide, not to necessarily -- well, you know, clearly weighing on -- on one ethnic group. But what I am here saying in this paragraph is that by April the Bosnian Serbs -- or sorry, the -- the JNA was assisting the Bosnian Serbs, and I highlight that that might actually have been -- that balance may not have been genuine, from the documentation I've seen in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's not what you say there. You say: "If it had genuinely existed."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, I didn't see it existing in 1991 either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I also, then, take it that you do not exclude for the possibility that it might have been existed, but from what you observed, you can make no final conclusions as to whether it existed or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the documentation I see in late 1991, I do not believe the JNA was operating in a completely balanced way. In the documentation that I've seen in 1991, I see references to protecting the Serbs against genocide. I see the arming of Serb volunteers, the use of Serb volunteers in Western Slavonia and Croatia. And I am arguing here that I am not sure, when you look at April 1992, that that necessarily was a balance at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that supports your doubts whether it ever existed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly from late 1991 and the war in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I'm not talking about the whole of the history, but ... Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in a -- a federal system from a military analyst's point of view, Mr. Brown, is it perhaps predictable that the federal institution might support a group that wanted to maintain that federal state?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't think I can answer that adequately, whether it's predictable or whether it's not, in terms of a hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, we have many examples through history, but we won't go through that at this point, in view of the limited time that I have. Now, let's look at -- further on in your report, where you deal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with the 16th Session in your report and you come to Mladic's contribution. You quote there in 1.45: "Some of the most striking comments made during the session indicating a clear understanding," et cetera, et cetera. You know the portion of the report I'm referring to and I won't read it through. You quote Mladic there. Then in the next paragraph, you say: "Even these comments, however, should be placed in some context. As one of those expected to implement the goals, he may well simply have not been more aware -- have been more aware of the practical limitations of what the Assembly were proposing." That, Mr. Brown, is pure speculation on your part, is it not? That is you trying to fit it in with your overall hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he himself says let's not set ourselves goals that we cannot achieve. I believe that's a phrase he uses somewhere in the Assembly -- or is it -- yes, page 34 of the translation I have, "Please let us not --" excuse me. "Please, let not us set before ourselves goals that will bring us down. Let us set before ourselves goals we can achieve."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he also goes on to say that he has reiterated that to the top leadership of the Serbian people at a meeting in Nevesinje he had sometime prior to this Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, the Trial Chamber will be able to read the 16th Session in its entirety and form their own views, and I don't have a great deal of time left for cross-examination. I'm not going to spend a lot of time on this, but where you put forward a view "he may well simply," there's an alternative view, isn't there? You must concede that.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's alternative views in -- in many issues, Ms. Loukas, but when I read his speech in entirety, when I see that he seems to be the only one uttering words of caution --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's your analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my analysis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And it's capable of more than one analysis. You would concede that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many things in life are open to different analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm not talking about many things in life, I'm talking about this.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not when I read it. I feel that he's one of the few, if any, that utters words of caution at the Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's your reading. Let's move on to another section of your report, where you indicate, in paragraph 1.60: "In summary, the goals articulated at the 16th Assembly Session shaped the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina from May 1992." Now, Mr. Brown, when you look at a statement like that, is it possible that you, as an expert employed by the Prosecution, are adopting a -- an approach that is based on attempting -- looking at the events that occurred and attempting to place them in your perspective in a way that does link the 16th Assembly Session to everything that happened? Are you prepared to concede that there's an alternative view, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the comment in section 1.60. I think there are clear indications from military documentation that tie in activities on the ground that the military conducted operations clearly in line with these strategic objectives. The documentations note that; the military operations themselves note that; and I would argue that you can tie these objectives to military operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And were shaping military -- certainly shaping military operations post this Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay, and -- sorry. You haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documentation indicates that. It's not -- it's not -- you know, it's my view of this documentation, reading of the documentation leads to that conclusion. And I think if you looked at the material in its entirety, you'd come to that conclusion too.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Brown, just in relation to that, part of the reason that you tie in the goals of the 16th Assembly Session with what occurred on the ground is that whenever you see the term "goal" in a military document, you automatically tie that in with the goals of the 16th Assembly Session; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not necessarily true. I look at all the material together. When a corps commander says "goals," he's a senior-level figure. He's talking at his level, which is a very high level. When I see references in directives that clearly link in operations in the Corridor, operations in Sarajevo, operations in the Drina Valley, Operational Directive 4, that seems to me very, very clear indications that these goals were not rarefied political statements made at the Assembly sessions that had no meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to the question of removal of Muslims from the army, I just want to deal with that question at -- at a certain point before I run out of cross-examination time. It's quite clear, is it not, that the issue of loyalty in what was perceived as a civil war was a very important issue, the loyalty of the soldiers. You'd agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, loyalty, presumably, in a military organisation is important, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So -- and there were, of course, examples of Muslims who were in the VRS playing the double game, as it were.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of those and I'm not quite sure what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Really? As a military analyst you're not aware of people being ostensibly on one side but assisting the other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you -- in your question, you specifically dealt with such a situation in the VRS. The witness said he was not aware, and then you asked more or less the same question but then not specifically to the VRS. Could you please clarify, where you said "Really? As a military analyst are you not aware of..." and now I translate it: Muslims being in the army but assisting not the army?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just looking for a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Let's deal with it another way. Combat readiness report, at page -- where is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The combat readiness report at page 80. Do you have that page?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It indicates about halfway down the page that "The national structure of active officers serving in the Army of Republika Srpska is 37 Montenegrins, 204 Yugoslavs, 62 Croats, 26 Macedonians, 33 Muslims, 13 Slovenes, 2.165 Serbs, three Albanians, one Bulgarian, two Czechs, four Hungarians, three Ruthenians, one Turk, one Jew, one Pole, one Roma, one Ukrainian, and 21 of undeclared nationality." So this report that's based on the activities of 1992 certainly shows that there were a significant proportion of non-Serbs in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll object to that, Your Honour. This doesn't talk about the number of non-Serbs in the army; it talks about active officers serving within the army. That's the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not sure I understand the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this talks -- this data that is presented to you is presented in respect of active officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The question that is put is a significant proportion of non-Serbs in the army in total. We know how many people there were in the army, which was a reference yesterday in terms of the size. That's on pages 70 and 71. This data doesn't relate to that. This data --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I see your point, Mr. Harmon. Well, it's -- a fortiori, it's even better; we're talking about the officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So a significant proportion of the officers in the VRS were non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's not all officers; it's active officers. And there were reserved and mobilised officers. And I think if you go to page 76 there --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, active officers are probably the most important, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: They're not important?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying they're not important. I'm not saying that they're not always the most important. I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So would that mean that if you would add that the inactive officers, that there were even more non-Serbs in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid it's a logical consequence, isn't it? If I have, well, let's say, 300 active officers of non-Serb origin, if you say, "Well, this is not just all the officers, it is just the active officers," if you would add the non-active officers, that either it would be the same or more. If there would be zero non-active officers, then it would be the same; if it would be more than zero, it would be more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would imagine it would be more than this. However, it tended to be that non-active officers who were reservists who were mobilised from municipalities and from areas. People who had served in the JNA who had retired or people who -- so I can't say whether it would be an equal number or I couldn't even tell you how many there was. But yes, I would imagine there -- there probably are some reserve, non-Serb officers or non-active mobilised officers in that figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I couldn't tell you the number and I couldn't necessarily agree that it would directly equate to the percentage here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could not be in these numbers because these numbers only deal with active officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whatever non-active officers there were should be added to get the total number of officers, active and non-active, in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so at all. You've got two municipalities, as I say, involved in -- with categorising people. There are three categories there. So I don't think that's tenuous at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go to paragraph 2.209 of your report. utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we -- if we look more broadly at Bosnia. I'm wondering if you've ever had the opportunity to read the book by Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You know who Mr. Sefer Halilovic is, do you not?

utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, it will probably help if I have my headphones on, I must say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. The international community bearing responsibility for the situation in Yugoslavia, I want to know your view. Is there anything in that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view or what the documents say?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Brown, let's go on to paragraph 2.238 of your report. utterances.text: Okay. Why is it that it's not insignificant, as opposed to significant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, before I ask you to continue, I'd like to draw -- ask your attention for the following matter: It has to do with the testimony of Mr. Davidovic. The Chamber is confronted with an issue of appropriateness of questions to the witness Davidovic. These questions went exclusively to the credibility of the witness and included serious allegations of misconduct. While a party may be fully justified to put such questions to a witness, it should not be done in the absence of reasonable grounds to believe that the witness did misbehave in the way that was put to him. The Defence has put to the witness in its questioning that: He was a criminal; that Mr. Davidovic gained money from transporting Muslims; that his unit stole money, beating and evicting civilians; that he stole material from the dental office of a Muslim; that he is subject to three criminal proceedings in Bijeljina; and that he profited from activities of seizing vehicles in Zvornik and Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If Your Honour has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm just pausing for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence submitted that there were reasonable grounds for the mentioned allegations and mentioned in this respect that it had been provided with certain information by their investigators, including the existence of a film of a woman alleging criminal conduct by the witness and other documentary evidence from before the beginning of the witness's testimony. The film had not arrived in time for the hearing and the Defence did not specify any further basis for the questioning. The Prosecution contested that such reasonable grounds existed. And in particular, after a few days, it provided the Chamber with the affidavits of one person mentioned as an alleged victim of the witness's criminal behaviour and of another person -- and of other persons apparently aware of the facts. It also highlighted the use by the Defence of the expression "criminal proceedings" when, in its submissions, no such proceedings had or were being underway. The questions to the witness had no direct bearing on questions of guilt or innocence of the accused. However, the Chamber is responsible for the integrity of the proceedings. As part of this responsibility, the Chamber needs to ensure that no witness, especially if he or she has given the testimony publicly, has reasons to feel he or she is unfairly treated by any party. The Chamber deems that the responsibility -- this responsibility requires it to make further inquiries if one party argues the absence of reasonable grounds for the allegations made by the other party against a witness, and it is only after such inquiries that the Chamber will be in a position either to dismiss the argument or to consider whether the matter needs to be pursued further. The Defence is therefore instructed to inform the Chamber by the 21st of July, 2005 of all information it had available that could shed light on the allegations of misbehaviour. The Chamber stresses that it wants to be informed of all information the Defence had available, whether this information supported the allegations or suggested that they were unsubstantiated. If the Defence does not wish to share this information with the Prosecution, it may either apply for being heard ex parte or provide this information in writing without disclosing it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I've -- I've heard what Your Honour has indicated, and I can indicate obviously there's some matters I do need to clear up immediately, and that is -- I think I indicated that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm a bit concerned about the time for today. If there are certain matters, let's, then, do it at the end of the hearing. I have a few other procedural matters as well. utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. The only point I would make, and I take on board --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's -- of course, if there's any mistake, whatever the cause may have been, which is of course another matter, then that perhaps we should consider. But let's not go any quicker, then. Let's first see what happens. Then are you ready to continue cross-examination? And we would ask the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, I think you've had the opportunity over the break to look at the document behind tab 86.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in that regard, of course, it's important to note for the Trial Chamber that the document emphasises, for example, at page 3 that "In some communities neither the military nor the civilian judiciary is functioning. Judges have not been elected, and in Bosanska Krajina, for instance, several thousand court cases have not yet been resolved." You'll note that portion in the document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says, yes, on that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And it's quite clear, is it not, that there was a situation of chaos certainly in the first few months of the war in that regard.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In regard to the judiciary? Is that ...? Or more widely?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, both in regard to the judiciary and more widely, but particularly in regard to the military judicial system.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not so sure that was necessarily the case for the military judicial process. I do know that in -- I think it was in July there was instructions about the establishment of military courts. I saw some --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's in July?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in July 1992, yes. And then there were other documents in 1992 appointing juror judges, and I know that the -- from looking at the court records, that the military court did begin to function from around August 1992. So I'm not sure that it was necessarily chaos in the military court system, whether he's referring to the civilian processes, I can't really comment. It's not really my area --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, it states there "Neither the military nor the civilian judiciary is functioning." And that's in July, you'll note. And in my question, it was that -- "It's quite clear, is it not, that there was a situation of chaos certainly in the first few months in that regard?" And your response basically confirmed that because you indicated July and August, July in relation to a document at -- the military system beginning to function in August. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'd add that it does say "in some communities." It doesn't say "in entirety," but in some communities. But I would accede that in May and June there was some -- "chaos" is their word -- I'm not so sure if I would say that was the case. They did begin to function pretty quickly after that, which would seem to indicate that they had some degree of -- or some ability to resurrect the military judicial process relatively quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In fact, it talks about "Judges receiving threats and being in fear."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in fact it talks about that "In some municipalities, Bosanska Krupa, Donji Vakuf, Kupres, Derventa, the courts do not function and hardened criminals are released from prison, which affects the establishment of the rule of law and the work of law enforcement organs."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So it was obviously a problem, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to have been a problem highlighted in this document by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, because he thought it was a problem.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem so from this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it was also indicated in that document that "It is a priority for both the national service and the crime investigation service to detect war crimes, provide documentation, on-site investigations, photos, expert testimonies, medical findings, and file criminal reports. Documents are also provided for war crimes committed by Serbs."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And so on your reading of the document, it's quite clear that this report on some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead, that this issue, as far as you can see from the document, was being taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to be an issue that was raised at the meeting. I'm not sure who all was present there, but it seems to be an issue that was being raised and discussed and is some significance undoubtedly for the Ministry of the Interior to be writing a report on it. So it is an issue that they're discussing about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And it's an important issue and they want to do something about it, from your reading of the document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they appear to be highlighting that it's a problem that they want to address.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. In addition, if you look at page 4, the last paragraph: "The minister particularly pointed out the determination to take action to ensure full constitutionality and legality by preventing crimes from being committed, not only by citizens but also by army soldiers and officers, active-duty and reserve police, and members of Internal Affairs organs and their superior officers who have committed crimes of any kind." Do you see that portion of the document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So it's quite clear that the issue is being taken very seriously from -- from any reading of the document, clearly, is it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly it's an issue that they're discussing and it is of some importance for them to be talking about it in that way, and replete with references there, of course. One would have to not necessarily take this document in isolation, but presumably -- I'm not an expert on the Ministry of the Interior and the police but presumably look at what actions, at all, if any, fell from this and -- and what happened in the -- in the weeks and months afterwards. So -- but to answer your question is it -- they seem to be taking it seriously here, yes, but they -- they could make comments here but you would have to presumably look and see what follow-up happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed. But, of course, the -- the fact that the issue is taken seriously is a significant matter from the reading of the document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it appears at face value to be -- to be that but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've now four or five times heard you say, Ms. Loukas, what is obvious from reading the document. And we have also four or five times heard that the witness agrees with that but at the same time has some difficulties to accept that as the whole of -- of -- of what he has studied. But if forced to limit himself just to the reading of this document that he would agree with you. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's accurate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, then, clear for the Chamber and it was already clear for the Chamber three or four times --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to leave that topic. I was just interested in the witness's reaction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- and the way he reads the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, we'll have a break for four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I understand, Your Honour. Yes. --- Break taken at 12.59 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, in the preparation of your report, did you consult any military analysts from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the different definitions in the Yugoslav context of the term "order, directive, and instruction"?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I have an understanding in military terms what "order, directive, and instruction" is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I understand that. Have you ever consulted a -- a book by Colonel Branislav Jovanovic, "Introduction to Military Command Theory," specifically in the Yugoslavian context?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Mr. Harmon -- no, I will first ask whether Mr. Krajisnik has any further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would have only a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, have you seen the statement given by the defence minister in 1997 to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 9th, 11th, and 12th of December, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember reading that statement, and it was a long time ago, so I cannot remember the contents of it now, so I -- I -- I remember reading it, I know, but I can't remember the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Would you find it useful if I gave you a copy of the statement now? Would you like to give some comments, or would you like to say in general terms whether you referred to it at all while making your own analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make reference to that particular witness statement in my analysis, and my analysis was based on documentary material, written documentary material, not witness testimony. And I state that at the beginning of the -- the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you think that it is not important to know how what was conceived of was actually carried out? Are you not interested in what the minister in charge at the time had to say about that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I'm interested what the minister had to say about that, but the remit I was given in relation to the report was to review documentary material, predominantly material taken from the 1st Krajina Corps archive, although other materials as well, and it was not within the remit of this report to include witness testimony in it, so it is not included there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the system of information that was impeccably organised, and you said that you had insight into transcripts from the meetings of the Presidency of Republika Srpska. Did you also have a look at specifically the transcript of the session of the Presidency held on the 17th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, I believe, use the word "impeccably organised." I said, I believe, that the communications were very good. And I did look at the minutes of the Presidency session on the 17th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could a copy of the transcript please be placed in front of the witness now. That is 007679935. I asked the Registry for that yesterday. I have just one copy. It is paragraph 6, so if you wish, you can place it on the overhead projector. I gave copies yesterday. So it's just paragraph or item 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could put it on the ELMO and if it's zoomed in such a way that the witness can read it on the screen, then -- could the legal officer please try to verify whether this is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will help the witness by reading paragraph 6. Could I just have it placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already asked the Registry for this, so perhaps I could read paragraph 6 from the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the ELMO. Please read it slowly, Mr. Krajisnik, so that the interpreters ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Provide as urgently as possible equipment for establishing radio communications with all command centres in order to ensure synchronised and unified command." Could the witness please comment on this. This is the 17th of June, so it is almost three months into the war.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem at face value to be a requirement to provide radio communications. Radio communications were not the only form of communications that were available, of course. And I think the combat analysis readiness report indicates that there were difficulties with radio communications in particular; i.e., that's not communications that involve a telephone, a telex, a courier, meetings, or any other form of communication but it's a radio communication. And I know there were some difficulties in trying to have communication -- radio communications in particular, in part because some of the communication hubs were either damaged or had been -- were in Central Bosnia. So I can only assume here what they're trying to do is to better facilitate the communications by this particular means, which is radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, for Your Honours' benefit, this document in English is found at tab 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Krajisnik, could you put your next question to the witness. At least, if I take it that you've finished your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You have used two documents having to do with communications. One is 009498887, sent by Mr. Milutin Vukelic to the Main Staff and the Presidency, and the reply of Mr. Mladic, 00820950, dated the 20th of June. As far as I could understand, you stated that this serves as an evidence that these documents were also sent to the Presidency of Republika Srpska. Am I right in concluding this? Was that your -- or rather, was your interpretation correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vukelic -- or the document that Colonel Vukelic signed is -- does have an addressee the Presidency and the Main Staff, and that would indicate to me that there -- there was a communication link, that he was able to send that document to the Presidency. The response clearly comes from the Main Staff, and I think the response is actually the 9th of June, it's not the 20th, but the response is from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: But did you verify whether this document had indeed arrived from the Presidency to Mr. Vukelic? Have you received confirmation of this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the document is the other way round; it's from the -- it's from the military to the Presidency. But I haven't got access to documentation from the Presidency that would verify that it was actually received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Witness: You had at your disposal the minutes of the Presidency sessions. If I were to tell you that I went through all of the minutes of the Presidency during the relevant period of time and was unable to find any confirmation that this document had ever reached the Presidency, would you be able to contradict this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't expect the minutes of the Presidency session necessarily to show or indicate whether this document arrived at the Presidency. I would presumably expect some ledger in the communications centre in Pale or some other location to find whether this document was -- was transmitted and received. I don't think it's the minutes of the Presidency particularly that you would -- you would necessarily find this. So if it's not in the Presidency minutes, I'm not surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yesterday you said something and I forgot to ask the question, but you said that you did not have access to the documentation of the Presidency. What do you mean exactly by that? Did you try to conduct some research at the Presidency and you were not authorised to do so? Is that the way we should understand what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not involved in analysing the work of the Presidency for this report, and so I was not focussing on whatever documentation the Office of the Prosecutor may have had in that respect. It didn't fall within the remit of the report necessarily at all, and -- and I didn't -- I didn't inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This morning you stated that you read the book by Mr. Owen, "The Balkan Odyssey"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the book by Mr. Owen. I have to say it was a number of years ago, I would imagine probably in 1998 or 1999, so it's been some time since I've read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be placed on the overhead projector. There is a short sentence that I would like to be read out. I have also previously provided a copy of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are -- we received a copy of the page. Yes, you may put it on the ELMO. It's a B/C/S version. We are aware that it's already on the record that the copies might not be exactly the same in every respect -- I mean the English and the B/C/S copy -- but which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. portion you'd like to draw the attention of the witness to, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the right, please. Could you move it to the right. All right. That's good. I have marked my copy of the document and I would like to read out the passage and then I would like the witness to comment this, with the Chamber's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we do not have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I think is page 72. Mr. Owen says: "The recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina represented, as was predicted by many, a pressure on the trigger for the official eruption of the war, which was boiling in the background before the recognition. The European Community and the United States committed a critical error because they continued on the path towards the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the spring of 1992 when all individual signs indicated that that would represent adding fuel to the fire that was already burning." My question is: Do you share the opinion of Mr. Owen after analysing the situation while conducting your research?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. I think that calls for a political judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this seems to be very much to represent a political opinion of the author of this book. It's -- but let's ask the witness: Are you in a position on the basis of the documentary study you made to comment on this political opinion, whether in support of it, whether in -- not in support of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this strikes me as being a very difficult question to -- to -- to answer, and I'm not sure I'm currently in a position to -- really to do so. It would require, I think, a lot of thought and there's a lot of overlapping issues even just contained in the phrase that he's used. So I don't -- I'm not really sure that I can -- I can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I would like to put another brief question to the witness. I apologise. I would like to ask you something regarding the 16th Session. I think that the 16th Session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska was explained in detail. I don't think it is necessary to refer to the document, but if you wish, I can do so. You have read the minutes of the 16th Session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska held on the 12th of May, 1992, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Did you read the appeal that was sent to the European Commission at the conclusion of the session? And this was something that was read by Mr. Nikola Koljevic. And in that appeal, it was stated that: "We accept the end of the war" and that they were all in favour of a political solution. I can refer to the political page, if you wish. 12049482, in the very beginning, where Mr. Koljevic addresses the Assembly. I only have, unfortunately, the version in Serbian. I could not give you the number of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you tell us, Mr. Krajisnik, approximately on what page it is in the B/C/S so that we could find our way through the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 43, Your Honour. There are several versions here. This is on page 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that should, in the English, be one or two pages from the end. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think it's page 55 and 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Where Mr. Nikola Koljevic speaks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I continue with my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This appeal or, rather, a letter sent to the European Community, does it indicate to you that the discussion was held as to give preference to the war option or the political option and that they wanted negotiations to continue until a political solution was found? And this is in the time period before the Corridor was severed, before any of the strategic objectives were implemented.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to me that Mr. Koljevic is laying out the Serbian position and submitting that position. I'm not sure I'd agree with necessarily some of the issues he talks about in there as being an absolute accurate reflection of what I saw from the documentation, but this seems to be the position that he is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Trial Chamber understood your reply, so would you allow me to repeat. Was that an appeal sent to the European Community showing that the Serb side was resolved to halt any combat and to continue negotiations until a political solution is achieved? Is that what it states?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it would state. But I'm not sure some of the underlying comments here are accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. All I asked you, whether it is stated in the letter. Let me ask you something else now. You said that in early April -- the Yugoslav People's Army, in early April of 1992, stopped treating all three sides equally and that it sided with the Serb side, as you have put it. Is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion was that there was a convergence between the JNA and the SDS certainly by April 1992 and that some manifestations of that convergence were the provision of weapons to Serbian volunteers, and in April 1992 as well the assistance in some areas in active combat operations on the sides of the Serb -- Serbs. So I would say that there was a convergence that certainly had manifested itself very openly in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Now, in relation to that question, please tell me this: Are you aware of the activity and of the order of the Muslim TO commander to block barracks, to block roads used by the JNA which in fact was a declaration of war on the JNA? Are you aware of this document, of this order issued in early April which exists among the OTP documentation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that instruction, and I believe it came sometime after the -- the activities in Bijeljina and Zvornik, and it would seem -- although that's not a feature of my report, that those issues were linked and -- and related. But I am aware of it but it's not a feature of -- of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I will put just one more question in order to leave some time for others, although I do have more questions on my list. When you were tasked with writing this analysis in relation to Momcilo Krajisnik, did you receive information that in the course of the trial Defence presented a thesis that the six strategic goals were actually derived from the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the question. The question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's irrelevant whether the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's -- if the witness would know it, you can ask whatever question on the subject and then he would, I take it, not rely on what was put as a thesis by the Defence, because that's a party position taken. But -- so therefore that's not a question you can put to the witness, which does not mean that you could not put any question to the witness in relation to the subject on whether there was any similarity or whether the one plan covered the other or whether it was the other way around. So this question is not to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The form of the question also, Your Honour. Just -- I note Mr. Krajisnik is under a misapprehension. He in his question says: "When you were tasked with writing this analysis in relationship to Momcilo Krajisnik --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noted that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that's not the case. This report was written in 2002 and it was at the request of Jo Korner, as Mr. Brown has testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if you have any question in this context, Mr. Krajisnik, you may put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Did anyone suggest to you in the course of your work to compare the six strategic goals to the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And to follow up on that: As for the split that you mentioned, would it be possible to draw up a map of three ethnic communities without dividing the territory?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not in a position to answer that, I don't think. I'm not sure quite what you mean in the question, and I'm not a political negotiator or have studied political issues, but I'm really not sure I could answer the question, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Trial Chamber. I will conclude, but I just need to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In order to create a map, is it necessary to make an internal demarcation or a division of territory in order to have three ethnic communities? You are a military expert and you know how -- you know the process of drawing up maps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm a military expert and I've served in the military and I know how to draw maps, but it's not got any relation to dividing countries into ethnic communities, so I'm not really sure that I've got an expertise in that area at all and I don't think any comment I would have would be anything more than -- than speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I have one question. That relates to the document that's found in tab 86. Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to page 6, the last paragraph. This paragraph -- in this paragraph there is reference to "prisons and round-up centres and investigation centres," and then at the last sentence in that paragraph, it says: "Special emphasis should be placed on the issue of relocating certain citizens, villages, et cetera, because this does not fall within the competence of the MUP, although efforts are being made to link it to the MUP." Do you have any observations or comments on that particular sentence, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they don't seem to be too critical about the issue of relocating people and they're trying to resolve that problem. And I would only argue that it seems to cut to a number of other documents that there are references to relocating. This one would just seem to say that, you know, "It's not really our job but we need to sort the problem out."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And on page 3, a portion of this report went to the president of the Presidency and the Prime Minister. There is a reference to "documents." I'm referring to page 3, four paragraphs from the bottom. "Documents are also provided for war crimes committed by Serbs." Do you have any comments on that particular sentence?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they seem to be aware that there either are documents or they're to be provided, but -- about war crimes being committed by Serbs. I can't really say much more than the sentence itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I have no additional questions, Your Honour. Thank you very much, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Hanoteau would have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you have your report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to direct your attention to page 27 of your report. At the top of the page - and you reminded us of that fact yesterday - at the top of that page, you mention the remarks of General Mladic, who called for some caution regarding the attitude taken towards the non-Serbian population. And I think I remember - I'm not quite sure - but I seem to remember that these words were spoken before the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later, further down on the same page, paragraph 1.48, you say: "Interestingly, General Mladic indicated that all this should remain as an internal secret and that the goals --" I suppose these are political goals -- "should be presented in an acceptable way." And then you quote your source in that respect. When you give that quote, I would like to know which document this quote comes from and at what -- what was the date when these words were spoken, if we compare that to the first declarations, to the declarations made before the Assembly. Because I couldn't -- I was not able to find the date when I looked at the footnote.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's contained within the same speech that Mladic gives at the Assembly session. It's a reference of the same speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's the same speech.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So once you read the entire speech, can you perceive that there's some sort of contradiction within the text, within the speech, or not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read General Mladic's speech many, many times. I have to say it's not the easiest one to follow at times. It's -- he drifts off in parts. And, on the one hand, you have that reference where he's in essence appearing to say, "We must guard this as our secret and we must present them in an acceptable way," which would indicate -- and also he appears to be acutely aware of what is being proposed here. He, from my reading of the minutes, seems to be the only one that is uttering these words of -- of caution. And yet, on the other hand, he indicates that, "We must protect what we're talking about." To all intents and purposes, that's his -- the gist of what he says. He also talks about -- he uses somewhat inflammatory language, fundamentalism and the likes. And he also takes his position as commander of the army and accepts it willingly and outlines his view of what the army should be doing. So there does seem to be this somewhat contradictory message which he puts out, which I can only present as such, but he speaks at the Assembly session, he seems to know what the Assembly session is about, he accepts his position as commander of the army. He remains in that position through the whole war. And so even though he may have these initial words of caution, he clearly fulfils his position and stays in that position through the whole war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I would like you to turn back to page 52, please. And in paragraph 1-120, you mention "criticisms levelled by the military, given some of the weaknesses of the civilian authorities." And among these weaknesses, you mention on the fifth line "[In English] The slow pace of paramilitary formations." [Interpretation] Can you follow me?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you read anything about these criticisms; i.e., the very slow manner in which the civilian authorities were dealing with the issue of the disarming of the paramilitaries? In document 199, is anything mentioned about this, anything about the way in which this is evolving and is the real desire of the civilian authorities questioned here in any way, real desire to see this disarmament actually take place?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the reference simply makes it noted that it's passed up to the Main Staff, as it's -- as it's quoted, that there is a slow response to the disarming of paramilitaries. It's something that had been discussed in -- in maybe other forums prior to this. Maybe it's of some note that this comes a few weeks before that larger document on paramilitaries is issued in July, in which they list the paramilitaries that are operating, their features and characteristics, and they state that paramilitaries should be integrated or put under control of the army if not disbanded and legal measures taken. So whether this comment and others may have been a facilitation in that document being produced, I can't say. In terms of this reference, I think it was just a remark in a daily combat report that General Talic was passing up to his superior command, and there were other references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, so there is no clear illustration of this unwillingness on the part of the civilian authorities to see this task through. In other words, in your report, there is no instance of this anywhere.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that reference, but I think I used the word "paramilitaries are a complex issue." I think that's a phrase I use in my own report. My overall feeling with paramilitaries is that there was a recognition that they were there. There was a clear understanding what they were doing. Some paramilitaries were linked to party affiliations. And the issue of paramilitaries was one about control and bringing them into the military, not about specifically, as I've discussed earlier, about their -- their actions in a way. It was -- it was about bringing them into -- not having competing militaries, not breaking the unity of the Serbs, not breaking the unity of the -- the military, not having competing factions that were clearly going to reflect badly on the SDS. That, for me, seemed to be of far more importance to them than actually prosecuting them, not putting them in the military, not giving them access to weapons, not allowing them to continue their -- their -- their activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, if I may: On page 133, in paragraph 2.198 [as interpreted], if I've understood you correctly, you concluded that "The non-Serbs were armed in a totally different way to the way in which the Serbs were armed"; paragraph 2.193.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Krajina, I would certainly agree with that. General Talic had the best-equipped corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. On the following pages, you explain all of this and you say why you can assert this and you also noted that during specific combat operations such-and-such a weapon was seized, which indicated clearly that there was no heavy weaponry. Is this a very comprehensive view of the battlefields in the territory which you were conducting your research in, or were there instances where you were able to demonstrate that the non-Serbs were much better equipped? In other words, was your survey a comprehensive one?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was as comprehensive as I could make it from the documentation I see. Even if you were to take the two areas where I believed the Croats and Muslim defences were -- well, A, had the longest time to prepare, and in some areas - for example, in Jajce - had particularly important territory which made defence very -- relatively easy; it's very hilly there, even if you look at the Corridor, which the Croats had taken in March and had been able to presumably prepare their defences for some period of time, that Corridor was retaken within ten days. Now, the only area where I really saw -- well, there was two areas but there was area in -- around Jajce which it took the VRS a longer time to capture. It took them from, I believe, April into October, but it is exceptionally hilly territory. There are only one or two routes in there. It's territory that favours the defender. It also had a significant Muslim and Croat population there. But that even fell in October. That's the only area that I -- I would argue that the defenders, the non-Serbs, had significant -- well, had an achievement in which they held off the attack for some time. There's only one very small other area, which would be that small pocket in Kotor Varos, but I know what happened to those individuals in the end, which was in November. They were -- when they tried to break out, they were captured and killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions triggered by the questions of the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then, Mr. Brown, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming -- usually I say "coming to The Hague," but you're not very far away, but for having answered the questions of the parties, of the Bench. And you're excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and patience, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Brown out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although I would wish now immediately for the technicians and the interpreters to stop, since we're not sitting tomorrow, I have to briefly deal with a few matters. I'll do it as quickly as I can. Nielsen exhibits which were not used in examination, the parties would consult on the relevance of the documents and inform the Trial Chamber as soon as possible. I just remind the parties that they should do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger and I discussed that recently, and we'll deal with that ASAP next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's a new term, "ASAP next week," yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know as soon as possible, but to put that already in the next week is new for me. D45. There was an exhibit which gave in the footnote an interpretation of part of the evidence contained in it. We've asked whether the OTP had any problem. They had no problem. If there are no further comments from the Defence, we will admit that exhibit as it is, with -- including this footnote in which it explains how certain matters are understood if witness is told certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the last thing -- that's -- as a matter of fact, the Chamber is already informed about what the Prosecution intended with Witness Kaiser because we are provided with two transcripts, one of 1998 and one of 1996. It was explained to us that the Prosecution intended to -- sought -- seeks admission of the transcript of 1998 in its entirety; therefore, we find no highlights because they want everything in. And for 1996, the highlighted parts, unfortunately, we received at that time a copy without highlights, but meanwhile the OTP has provided the Chamber with a CD with the highlights on it. Is this -- I think this was not yet said in Court. That's where we have to deal with evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's a witness that Mr. Stewart was dealing with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- so I think it's best that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you'd pass this information to him --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that the Chamber now received the -- on the 13th of July the highlighted transcript of the 1996 transcripts. And if there would be any further comment on that, we'd like to hear that; otherwise, we'll take a decision on admission. As you may be aware, we could not take any decision if it was not clear what exactly was sought to be admitted. These were the procedural issues I would have.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's just one further issue I need to deal with, just in terms of this witness, and that is that, as I indicated yesterday, Your Honour - and I just want to foreshadow to Your Honours - Mr. Harmon and I have agreed on the tender of the transcript in relation to the evidence of this witness in the trial against Mr. Brdjanin. I can also indicate that one matter -- there were some matters raised in cross-examination that the witness was asked to go away and get further information in relation to, and there's also a document in relation to that, so that sometime during next week I can hand up to Your Honours the transcript from the Brdjanin trial in addition that this document that Mr. Harmon and I have discussed. And the only remaining matter is this -- I think that your assistant Mr. Acquaviva might be interested in this -- and that is just the material in relation to 280. Would you like that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask Mr. Acquaviva whether we'd like it now or as soon as possible next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could receive it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that your assistant was somewhat anxious for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We would then -- have we provided already provisional exhibit numbers or not? Otherwise, we will ask -- we have not done that yet. We'll ask the registrar to prepare the -- to give exhibit numbers, to prepare that and deal with it next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can indicate, Your Honour, that Mr. Gaynor and I have discussed this issue. There is, in fact, four documents: Two e-mails that Mr. Gaynor sent me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- in relation to Rule 68 material, a further translation from the Prosecution, and a memo prepared by my case manager in relation to the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's the four documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will then be sorted out. And then they'll get their description, they will get their numbers, and as soon as that's completely prepared, we'll come back to it in Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to tidy up that remaining loose end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know we're in a hurry. There is the issue of the exhibits that have been tendered. We can deal with those next week, the three binders and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would rather do that next week and not ask further -- anything further from the patience of the technicians and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No problem. The most important issue is an issue that Mr. Gaynor will address, and that is an issue regarding protective measures regarding KRAJ 682. There has been apparently an agreement between the parties, but Mr. Gaynor is in a position to briefly - quite briefly - inform the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that. If the parties have agreed on any issue, you also could send an e-mail to the legal officers, explain what the agreement is, send a copy to either Ms. Loukas or Mr. Stewart, and we usually consult our e-mails, so -- we'll then be aware of it, and then it can be dealt with in open Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, when we regulate these issues of exhibits, I will be filing also -- or tendering a contextual document that relates to Mr. Brown's testimony. I'm going to serve it on the Defence today and I will move it into admission next week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, you'll receive it and we'll hear from you if there are any objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm happy to look at yet another contextual document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This concludes today's hearing. We will adjourn and -- until next Monday, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II.
